title: What's in a surname?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and origins of surnames. They cover why surnames arose (population growth, travel, property and legal needs, nobility and rulers tracking people), early examples from China's Zhou dynasty and Roman naming systems, William the Conqueror's Domesday Book, and the main categories of surnames: place names (toponymic), topographic names, occupational names (including feminine forms like Brewster and Baxter), patronymic and matronymic names, nicknames, and actors taking character names. They discuss Welsh and Scottish/Irish prefixes (ap, Mac), Icelandic patronymics and the non-binary "-bur" option, Arabic ibn/bin naming (Saddam Hussein's full name), Jewish nature-based surnames in Austro-Hungary, surnames given to freed enslaved people after emancipation, marriage-related name changes and hyphenated names (Spain's double surnames, Lucy Wainwright Roach, Jeffrey Hammond), and the myth that Ellis Island officials changed immigrants' names. The episode closes with a listener mail from Lyle correcting their probability math on the church choir coincidence.

segments.title: Opening banter and origin of Clerk/Bryant
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of surnames, joke about the origins of their own last names (Bryant meaning wagon driver or builder), and tease Ed's Polish surname.

segments.title: When and why surnames arose
segments.summary: Surnames emerged much later than given names, around the eleventh century in England and Western Europe, with earlier examples in China and Rome. Population growth, travel, property, titles, and rulers' need to track people drove their adoption. William the Conqueror's Domesday Book helped formalize the custom.

segments.title: Humorous medieval surnames and Roman three-name system
segments.summary: Medieval England produced crude nicknames that became surnames, and sarcastic names like Goodman existed. The Roman system used praenomen, nomen, and cognomen, and surnames later reappeared with Europeans.

segments.title: Asian surname order
segments.summary: Korean, Japanese, and Chinese names are traditionally written surname first, and Japan formally moved to this convention in recent years.

segments.title: Place name and topographic surnames
segments.summary: Surnames derived from places of origin (toponymic, such as d'Arcy from Arcy in Normandy) and from natural features (topographic, such as Hill, Green, Bay, Shore, Western, Ireland). Nobles took place names when they went to court; commoners rarely did.

segments.title: Occupational surnames
segments.summary: Occupations are a very common source of English surnames, such as Smith, Carpenter, Weaver, Clark, and Thatcher. Medieval feminine suffixes (-ster) produced names like Brewster and Baxter. Surnames from occupations after the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries are rare, as the practice solidified.

segments.title: Actors' stage names and nickname surnames
segments.summary: Actors sometimes took surnames of characters they often played, such as King or Lord. Early given names began as nicknames, sometimes crude, such as Shakespeare or Wagstaff.

segments.title: Patronymic and matronymic names
segments.summary: Patronymic names derive from a father's name (Johnson, Smithson, Martin, MacDougal). Matronymic names such as Marriott are rarer. Icelandic naming uses patronymics that differ between siblings, such as Björk Guðmundsdóttir.

segments.title: Icelandic non-binary naming and Arabic naming
segments.summary: Iceland added a third option, -bur, for non-binary people. Arabic names use ibn/bin for son of and bint for daughter of, across several generations; Saddam Hussein's full name is given as an example.

segments.title: Welsh and Scottish/Irish prefixes
segments.summary: Mac in Scottish and Irish names means son of; in Wales ap means son of, and over time ap truncated to become names like Price from ap Rice.

segments.title: Name changes, hyphenation, and Ellis Island myth
segments.summary: Discussion of name changes: Jewish nature-based names in Austro-Hungary, surnames given to freed enslaved people after emancipation, marriage name conventions and hyphenated names (Spain's double surnames, the hosts' family examples, Jeffrey Hammond of Jethro Tull), and the myth that Ellis Island officials changed names, which the hosts say was largely untrue.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up, invite listener stories, and sign off.
